title: Getting under the skin and into the heart: Effects of parental tone of voice on adolescents' affective, behavioral, and physiological stress responses
abstract: Abstract How parents speak (their tones of voice) may matter as much as what they say. Although the role of parental control, relative to autonomy support, has been extensively studied, far less attention has been paid to whether adolescents distinguish between controlling and autonomy‐supportive tones of voice and whether such differences affect their affective, behavioral, and physiological stress responses. The present research employed an experimental, multimethod approach to address these gaps. A pilot study among Dutch‐speaking adolescents in Belgium ( N = 42, M age = 14.69 years; 85.7% boys) established perceptual differentiation between controlling and autonomy‐supportive voices, with a controlling tone of voice causing higher self‐reported stress and reduced satisfaction of basic needs for autonomy and relatedness. The main study, also conducted among Dutch‐speaking adolescents in Belgium ( N = 103, M age = 14.27 years; 54.4% boys) replicated and extended this pattern by showing that a controlling tone of voice elicited higher stress, lower autonomy and relatedness satisfaction, greater defiance, and increased resentment toward the speaker. Physiological findings were more tentative and limited to RMSSD (the root mean square of successive differences), a broad metric of heart rate variability (HRV), for which decreases from baseline to exposure to the controlling tone were observed. However, changes in RMSSD did not differ significantly between conditions. No robust moderation effects of perceived parenting style were observed. These findings suggest that adolescents are sensitive to tone of voice, particularly in their affective responses and behavioral intentions, with some preliminary evidence for physiological responding.
